title: Two travelers in the forest
hookLine: two travelers left behind in a forest, one who can't walk and one who can't see
tomorrow: Why does the dancer leave the stage?

lines: ONE CAN'T WALK, ONE CAN'T SEE.
cards: A caravan has been scattered in a forest, and two travelers are left behind. One can't walk. The other can't see.

Night is coming. The one who can't walk can see the path, the river, the way out, but he can't take a step. The one who can't see has strong legs and a strong back, but he has no idea which way to go.

Alone, both of them stay in the forest. The classic commentaries on the Samkhya Karika tell this little story, and the Karika itself names it in a single phrase. Today it explains how the whole world got moving.

teach.b: Here's the ending. The traveler who can't see lifts the other onto his shoulders. Now one does the walking and the other does the seeing, and together they get out of the forest.
Once they reach the village, they go their separate ways. The Karika uses this picture for the two from Samkhya's opening days.
Prakriti is the one with legs: she moves, changes and unfolds, but she has no seeing of her own. Purusha is the one with eyes: the witness, who sees but never acts.
Their coming together, the verse says, is like the lame and the blind, and creation unfolds from that meeting. And the Karika says what the meeting is for.
It's so that purusha can see prakriti, and so that purusha can finally be set free.

In Samkhya the world isn't an accident, and it isn't a trap someone built. Here is the teaching, plainly: in Samkhya the world exists for the self, first for experience, then for freedom. Notice too how the story ends.
The two travelers part ways. That's where Samkhya is heading. Not everyone in the Hindu tradition tells the end of the journey this way.
Vedanta, at the close of this season, has its own account. A partnership that neither side could manage alone, that gets somewhere, and then lets go.

how: Teachers of Samkhya and of Yoga philosophy explain the meeting of purusha and prakriti with the story of the lame man and the blind man, drawn from the Karika's phrase and its commentaries.

o: a folk tale about two brothers lost in a forest
verses that picture seer and seen as two travelers
a poem in praise of a holy river's journey

p: so purusha can see, and be freed

s: in Samkhya, prakriti can see but not move
it's the other way around: prakriti moves and unfolds; purusha sees.
the Karika says the meeting of purusha and prakriti has a purpose
so that purusha can see prakriti, and be set free.

games.q: you're the traveler who can't see, with strong legs, lost in the forest next to someone who can't walk. what do you do?
o: set off alone and hope for the best.
lift him onto your shoulders and let him guide.
wait for the caravan to come back.
games.why: one carries, one guides, and together they get out. the Karika uses it for prakriti and purusha.

practice: Rest one hand on your knee, lift it a little and lower it again, a few times: the hand is the one with legs, and it moves.

Then notice the seeing, aware of the movement without lifting anything, and let the hand go still: let the body carry, let the seeing see. If you pray, you can offer thanks for the body that carries you.

wordCard.voice: The Samkhya Karika. Its picture of the world's beginning: prakriti, who moves but can't see, and purusha, who sees but can't move, getting out of the forest together.

orig.note: Sanskrit: in Samkhya, the root of everything seen, the one that moves and unfolds.

carryVoice: Your line: prakriti moves, purusha sees. One carries, one guides, and together they get out. That's today, done.
